title: Can You Just Shut Up?
author: Daily Stoic
summary: This short Daily Stoic essay argues that the instinct to respond immediately, to demonstrate knowledge or solve a problem quickly, actively prevents genuine listening, drawing on Marcus Aurelius's discipline of entering as much as you can into the mind of the speaker as the ancient version of a skill modern conversation rarely practices. It uses biographer Robert Caro's interviewing technique as a concrete modern application: Caro trained himself to write SU (Shut Up) in his notebook whenever tempted to fill an interview subject's silence, discovering that a few seconds of unfilled quiet does more to draw out real information than any follow-up question. The piece frames silence itself as an active tool rather than a passive gap, arguing that most people's discomfort with pauses causes them to volunteer information, correct themselves, or elaborate, precisely the material a good listener needs, as long as the listener isn't the one who breaks first. The essay's practical takeaway is that genuine listening requires actively suppressing the urge to prepare a response while the other person is still speaking.
points: The essay's central technique, Robert Caro's habit of writing SU (Shut Up) in his notebook to resist filling silence during interviews, turns an abstract listening virtue into a concrete, repeatable practice.

Its key reframe treats silence as an active tool rather than an awkward gap, arguing that silence and people's need to fill it is what draws out real information, provided the interviewer isn't the one who breaks first.

The piece connects ancient Stoic practice, Marcus Aurelius's discipline of entering into the mind of the speaker, directly to a specific twentieth-century biographer's method, giving the philosophical claim a concrete, verifiable modern application.

Its underlying diagnosis, that rehearsing your next response while someone is still talking is itself a form of not listening, reframes good listening as an act of restraint rather than simply a matter of attention.
quotes: Before they finish their sentence, we're ready with our response. Ready to show how smart we are, how much we know, or how quickly we can solve the problem.

Marcus Aurelius reminded himself to do just that, saying that he needed to get into the habit of listening attentively to anything that anyone says, and enter, as much as you can, into the mind of the speaker.
To enter into another person's mind, even for a moment, we first need to get out of our own head. We have to stop rehearsing our answer. Stop preparing the clever thing we're going to say next.

When I'm waiting for the person I'm interviewing to break a silence by giving me a piece of information I want, I write SU (for Shut Up!) in my notebook. If anyone were ever to look through my notebooks, he would find a lot of SUs there.
Silence is the weapon, Caro said, silence and people's need to fill it, as long as the person isn't you.
